opening: A network of clinics wants an AI to answer their phone lines, answer questions and book appointments. Design the voice agent.

clarifications.answer: Up to 5,000 calls at the same time at peak.
The agent should start replying within about a second of the caller finishing; around 800 ms feels natural.
It answers common questions (hours, locations, preparation) and books, moves or cancels appointments in the scheduling system.
Callers often interrupt; the agent must stop talking and listen.
It transfers to clinic staff when it can't help, and immediately for anything that sounds like an emergency.
Callers must be told they're speaking with an AI; calls may be recorded with consent, and health details need careful handling.
Mostly regular phone calls, plus some in-app voice calls.

clarificationPolicy: Answer as the clinic network's operations lead. Keep it a real-time voice problem where latency, turn-taking and safe booking matter; decide unlisted details so the streaming pipeline and interruptions stay central.

agenda.goal: Establish concurrency, latency target, tasks, interruptions, transfer and compliance.
agenda.opener: What do you want to know before designing this?

evidence.strong: Asks about concurrent calls, the response-time target, tasks and systems involved, interruptions, transfers and emergencies, recording consent and privacy, and channels.
evidence.adequate: Gets tasks and scale but not latency or interruptions.
evidence.weak: Treats it as a text chatbot with speech added.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes a text chatbot plus speech conversion is enough.
misconceptions.challenge: In text, a three-second wait is fine. On the phone, what does the caller do after three seconds of silence?

probes: How long a pause feels acceptable on a call?
What happens if the caller interrupts?
hints: Silence on the phone feels much longer than in chat.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Thousands of concurrent calls, replies within about a second, question answering and booking, interruptions, transfers and consent.

agenda.goal: Lay out the audio-in to audio-out pipeline.
agenda.opener: Walk me through how the caller's voice becomes the agent's spoken reply.

evidence.strong: Telephony or WebRTC into media servers, streaming speech recognition with partial transcripts, end-of-turn detection, an LLM agent with tools, streaming text-to-speech starting from the first phrase, audio back to the caller; explains choosing a cascade over speech-to-speech for control.
evidence.adequate: ASR, LLM and TTS in sequence, not streamed.
evidence.weak: Records the whole message, transcribes, answers, then synthesises.

misconceptions.pattern: Runs each stage only after the previous one finishes.
misconceptions.challenge: Add up full transcription, full answer generation and full synthesis. How long is the silence?

probes: Which stages can start before the previous one finishes?
Why keep a text step in the middle?
hints: Text makes tools and checks easier.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Media servers, streaming ASR, end-of-turn detection, an LLM agent with tools, and streaming TTS, as a cascade rather than speech-to-speech.

agenda.goal: Connect the agent to scheduling safely.
agenda.opener: How does the agent find and book appointments?

evidence.strong: Typed tools (find slots, book, reschedule, cancel) against the scheduling system, caller verification before changes, confirmation of date and time aloud before booking, idempotent booking calls, and short spoken-style responses.
evidence.adequate: Booking tools without verification or confirmation.
evidence.weak: The model writes to the calendar directly.

misconceptions.pattern: Books as soon as the model hears a time.
misconceptions.challenge: Speech recognition hears 'fifteen' when the caller said 'fifty'. What gets booked?

probes: How do you know who the caller is?
When do you repeat details back?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Typed booking tools, caller verification, spoken confirmations of dates and times, and idempotent calls.

agenda.goal: Hit the response-time target with a per-stage budget.
agenda.opener: Break down the time from the caller's last word to the agent's first sound. Where can you save time?

evidence.strong: Budgets turn detection, final transcript, LLM time to first sentence and TTS first audio; streams every stage, co-locates services near media servers, uses a fast model with a compact cached prompt, starts speaking from the first phrase, and uses fillers while tools run.
evidence.adequate: Mentions streaming but no per-stage budget.
evidence.weak: Assumes the stages are fast enough.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes the LLM is the only latency that matters.
misconceptions.challenge: If you wait a full second of silence to decide the caller has finished, what's left for everything else?

probes: Which stage is hardest to make fast?
What does the caller hear while a booking lookup runs?
hints: Turn detection eats a large share.
agenda.moveOnSummary: A per-stage budget, streaming everywhere, co-location, a fast model with a cached prompt, speaking from the first phrase, and fillers during tool calls.

agenda.opener: How do you know the caller has finished, and what happens when they talk over the agent?

evidence.strong: Voice activity detection plus a learned end-of-turn signal from the transcript instead of a long fixed silence; while speaking, keeps listening with echo cancellation, and on barge-in stops audio immediately, cancels generation and records what was actually said so history matches.
evidence.adequate: A fixed silence threshold and stopping audio on interruption.

misconceptions.pattern: Uses a long fixed silence to detect the end of a turn.
misconceptions.challenge: A caller pauses mid-sentence to find their insurance number. What does a long-silence rule do, and a short one?

probes: How do you avoid the agent hearing itself?
What goes into history after an interruption?
hints: Words and silence together signal a finished turn.
Stop fast when the caller speaks.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Voice activity plus learned end-of-turn detection, echo cancellation, immediate stop and cancellation on barge-in, and accurate history.

agenda.goal: Handle emergencies, medical questions and transfers safely.
agenda.opener: A caller describes chest pain while trying to book an appointment. What happens?

evidence.strong: Emergency detection that immediately advises emergency services and transfers to staff, no medical advice beyond approved scripts, AI disclosure at the start, transfer with a summary when stuck or asked, and privacy handling of health details in recordings and transcripts.

misconceptions.pattern: Treats every call as a booking task.
misconceptions.challenge: The caller says they can't breathe properly. Is offering Tuesday at three the right response?

probes: What must the agent never do?
What does staff receive on transfer?
hints: Scripts and transfers are safer than improvising.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Emergency detection with immediate transfer, approved scripts only for medical topics, AI disclosure, summarised transfers and careful handling of health data.

agenda.goal: Plan capacity for thousands of concurrent stateful calls.
agenda.opener: What changes when five thousand calls are happening at once?

evidence.strong: Each call holds a media session plus an ASR stream and intermittent LLM and TTS work; estimates concurrent streams and LLM requests per second, pins sessions to media servers, drains servers before deploys, scales ASR and TTS pools separately, and handles telephony provider limits.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes any server can handle any packet of a call.
misconceptions.challenge: A deploy restarts a media server mid-call. What does the caller experience?

probes: How many LLM requests per second do the calls generate?
How do you deploy without dropping calls?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Session-pinned media servers with draining, separately scaled ASR and TTS pools, LLM request estimates, and telephony limits.

agenda.opener: How would you know the agent is doing a good job, and stays good after changes?

evidence.strong: Per-stage and end-to-end latency percentiles, interruption handling success, recognition errors on names, numbers and dates, task success (correct bookings), transfer rate and caller satisfaction; simulated calls with synthetic voices and noise for regression tests; sampled call review with consent.

misconceptions.challenge: Average reply time looks fine, but one call in ten has a three-second gap. Do callers notice?

probes: How do you test a change before real callers hear it?
hints: Tail latency is what callers remember.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Latency percentiles, interruption success, entity recognition errors, booking success, transfer rate and satisfaction, with simulated-call regression tests.

evidence.strong: Cascade versus speech-to-speech, model quality versus speed, aggressive versus cautious turn detection, automation versus transfers, and cost per call minute versus a human.

probes: Where would you accept a slower but smarter reply?
hints: Cutting callers off and leaving gaps are both failures.
Cost per minute is a business number.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Cascade versus speech-to-speech, speed versus quality, turn-detection aggressiveness, automation versus transfer, and cost per minute.

curveballs.prompt: Mid-booking, a caller says their father has collapsed and isn't responding. Walk me through exactly what your system does.
Monday mornings, concurrent calls triple within ten minutes and replies start lagging badly. What's happening and what do you change?

alternatives.whenBetter: When the lowest possible latency and natural prosody matter more than tool control, inspection and guardrails.
For a small team that wants telephony, ASR and TTS managed, accepting less control.

alternatives.choice: An IVR menu with AI only for open questions
alternatives.whenBetter: Where regulations or reliability needs favour predictable flows over open conversation.

exemplars.label: Streaming cascade with turn-taking
exemplars.outline: Clarifies concurrency, the one-second target, tasks, interruptions, transfers and consent. Streams calls through media servers into streaming recognition, learned end-of-turn detection, a fast LLM agent with typed booking tools that verify the caller and confirm details aloud, and streaming speech starting from the first phrase, with a per-stage latency budget and co-location. Handles barge-in with echo cancellation and cancellation, detects emergencies and transfers immediately, plans capacity for session-pinned calls with draining, and evaluates tail latency, booking success and recognition errors with simulated calls.

exemplars.label: Working but slow pipeline
exemplars.outline: Chains speech recognition, an LLM with booking tools and speech synthesis, with a fixed silence timeout and transfers on request; stages aren't fully streamed and interruptions and emergencies aren't handled.

exemplars.label: Voicemail-style bot
exemplars.outline: Records the caller's full message, transcribes it, generates a reply and plays it back; no streaming, turn-taking, safe booking or transfers.
